Beavers in the Low Countries: Where Does the Risk Arise?

MSc research project — agent-based modelling of beaver burrowing behaviour in R

Author

Emiel van Loon, Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics (IBED), University of Amsterdam

Published

October 1, 2026

At a glance. We are looking for one or two MSc students Biological Sciences who are interested in studying beaver behaviour through computational toos. Activities include: re-implementing and extending an agent-based model of beaver behaviour in R, testing it against newly collected field and telemetry data, and applying it to explore where in the Dutch lowlands beaver burrowing creates real risks for dikes, railways and roads.

Why this project?

In 1988 the Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber) was reintroduced in the Netherlands, after being absent since the 1820s. Since then the population has grown rapidly and now numbers several thousand animals spread over almost all provinces (BIJ12, 2017). Beavers are a strictly protected species and ecosystem engineers: they create wetlands, raise biodiversity and can buffer water flows (Brazier et al., 2021).

But beavers also dig. In the flat, heavily engineered Dutch delta, a burrow in a dike, a railway embankment or a road verge may weaken that structure. The risk is greatest during high water, when animals are forced out of their normal burrows and look for dry places, sometimes by digging into the very levees that protect people from flooding (Berg & Natarajan, 2023; Berg & Noyons, 2024). Water boards, Rijkswaterstaat and ProRail now spend large amounts of money and staff time on inspections, repairs and preventive measures. Much of what we know about beaver biology comes from other kinds of landscape, so it cannot simply be applied to the Dutch lowlands. Risk assessments are therefore still largely based on expert judgement (Jansen, 2026).

The larger research project

This MSc project is part of a national, multi-partner research project, “Graverij door bevers en (water-)veiligheid” (RAAK-Publiek), led by Hogeschool Van Hall Larenstein, together with the Zoogdiervereniging, several water boards (Brabantse Delta, WDOD, Rivierenland), STOWA, Deltares, Rijkswaterstaat, ProRail, HZ University of Applied Sciences and the University of Amsterdam. The project collects new data in two Dutch study areas:

  • GPS/radio telemetry of about 24 tagged beavers, plus wildlife cameras, to learn how individual animals use the landscape during low and high water (Loonstra, 2026);
  • A national database of burrow locations (2020–2025) collected by water boards and ProRail, harmonised and calibrated in the field;
  • Hydrological, vegetation and terrain data for the study areas.

Your project is the modelling component of this effort: it turns field data into a tool that managers can use to ask “what if?” questions.

The main question

Where and under which conditions does beaver burrowing arise in the Dutch lowlands, and how can an agent-based model help us understand, predict and reduce the associated risks?

Understanding this better lets infrastructure managers focus inspections and preventive measures where they matter most, without unnecessary interventions in a protected species.

Starting point: an existing model

Deltares built a first agent-based model (ABM) in NetLogo to explore how beaver families behave when a river rises (Berg & Natarajan, 2023; Berg & Noyons, 2024). In a stylised floodplain with a river, levees, trees and shrubs, each beaver family (and competitors such as badgers) decides whether to dig and where to seek safety, depending on the water level, how long the high water lasts, windchill, the available energy and the presence of other animals. The output is a probability of digging into the levee, used as a proxy for risk. The model is documented with the ODD protocol (Grimm et al., 2020) and is a proof of concept: it shows that this kind of model can generate useful insight, and it lists what is missing, namely realistic landscapes, vegetation, age classes and dispersing animals, territories, underwater digging, and comparison with observations.

Aims of the project

You will work towards three connected aims.

1. Re-implement and improve the existing ABM in R

  • re-implement the Deltares model in R using either (functions from) existing packages like abmR (Gochanour et al., 2023) or as a stand-alone package, following the ODD protocol (Grimm et al., 2020; Railsback & Grimm, 2019);
  • make the model more realistic by working through the recommendations of the original report: realistic (GIS-based) landscapes instead of a conceptual world, variable vegetation, territories, age classes and dispersing individuals, and the ability to dig below the water line;
  • use the new telemetry and burrow data to decide which model structure and which parameter values make sense. Other beaver ABMs may offer inspiration for the architecture of the model (J. R. M. Kennedy et al., 2026; Oliva et al., 2026), as well as research into when and where beavers build (J. Kennedy et al., 2024).

2. Validate the model with the project data

  • use about half of the field data to calibrate the model structure and parameters, and keep the other half for validation, following the principle of pattern-oriented modelling (Grimm & Railsback, 2012);
  • compare simulated space use and burrowing with the telemetry tracks (Loonstra, 2026) and with observed burrow locations and risk maps for the study areas, such as the GIS-based analysis for motorways by Jansen (2026);
  • analyse the sensitivity of the model and quantify its uncertainty.

3. Run scenario analyses

  • use the validated model to predict beaver behaviour under realistic high-water events in the coming years;
  • compare at least three scenarios from the project’s action perspective: (1) proactive measures that prevent or steer burrowing (from hard, digging-resistant structures to nature-based solutions such as artificial high-water refuges), (2) reactive measures such as targeted inspection and quick repair, and (3) keeping beavers away entirely, included as a reference only, since it conflicts with the goal of sustainable coexistence with beavers;
  • identify where in the landscape risks arise and how effective each scenario is at reducing them. Stakeholders will use these results to evaluate costs, effectiveness and social acceptance.

What you will deliver

  • a documented, open-source R implementation of the improved ABM, with technical documentation;
  • a thesis (MSc report) which will include a review of the relevant literature, sections on model building and validation and a scenario analysis for the study areas;
  • where possible, co-authorship of a scientific paper and the opportunity to present your results at a stakeholder symposium.

What we are looking for

Required

  • basic analytical skills (data analysis, statistics, structured thinking about models);
  • basic knowledge of R;
  • an interest in computational research and modelling.

Helpful, but not required

  • experience with simulation or agent-based modelling (for example with NetLogo);
  • experience with spatial data (rasters, GIS);
  • an interest in animal behaviour, ecology, or water management.

You will learn agent-based modelling in practice, how to publish reproducible models (ODD, open code) and how to work with real field data and practice partners. No previous knowledge of beavers is needed.

What this project offers

  • A topical, societally relevant research question with a direct link to practice;
  • Supervision by the University of Amsterdam (IBED), in close collaboration with Deltares, and the Zoogdiervereniging.
  • Access to unique, newly collected telemetry and burrow data.
  • A network of water boards, Rijkswaterstaat, ProRail and researchers.

Interested?

Send a short motivation and an overview of your study background (the courses you took in your MSc so-far and perhaps your BSc) to Emiel van Loon (e.e.vanloon@uva.nl). Practicalities (start date, number of ECTS, and exact team of supervisors) are to be agreed.

Note: some of the key sources, such as the reports by Jansen (2026), Loonstra (2026) and BIJ12 (2017), are in Dutch.
